Topic: When a government claims to derive its authority from the consent of the governed, yet denies the governed any practical mechanism to withdraw that consent, by what principle does it distinguish itself from tyranny?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
The question before me is whether the rhetoric of consent, stripped of its mechanism, constitutes legitimacy — or merely its more sophisticated counterfeit.

I observed in the Roman republic what consent actually requires: the tribunes, the veto, the capacity of the people to resist. Remove those instruments and you have not consent but flattery directed upward, a prince asking his subjects to applaud their own captivity. The word "consent" without the power of refusal is a confession disguised as a principle — it tells you what the ruler fears, not what the people hold. A government that permits no practical withdrawal of consent has simply concluded that the lion's method is safer than the fox's, while still wearing the fox's skin.

By no principle does it distinguish itself from tyranny. It *is* tyranny, dressed for a later century.

*The mask of consent, worn over the face of force, does not change the face — it only postpones the reckoning.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
The question is whether authority without accountability is still authority, or merely force wearing borrowed clothes — and I have thought on this longer than most men care to.

Men quit the state of nature not for love of their sovereign but from terror of one another; they surrender rights in exchange for protection, and that bargain is the whole foundation. When a government invokes consent as its title yet extinguishes every avenue by which consent might be revisited, it has retained the word while destroying the substance. Consent is not a deed signed once and irrevocable — it is a living compact renewed by the continuous fact of protection delivered. What collapses the distinction from tyranny is precisely this: the sovereign who cannot be checked when he fails to protect has severed the only chain that bound his authority to anything beyond appetite.

A government is distinguished from tyranny by performance, not proclamation.

*The covenant purchases peace, not submission; where peace is absent and redress forbidden, only the name of sovereignty remains.*
Keynes — Judgement:
The question of consent is not philosophical abstraction but institutional mechanics — like a currency, it retains value only insofar as convertibility into something real remains guaranteed.

I have long held that the distinction between liberty and its counterfeit lies not in ceremonial declarations but in operative instruments. A government that invokes the consent of the governed while eliminating every practical mechanism for withdrawing it has not transcended coercion — it has merely dressed coercion in democratic costume. The governed, in such a state, resemble investors holding irredeemable bonds: they possess the nominal form of a right while being denied all substance of it. Sovereignty claimed but never returnable is sovereignty stolen.

No principle distinguishes such a government from tyranny. It is tyranny with better public relations.

*The franchise without the power of recall is a promissory note the issuer has already decided never to honour.*
Hayek — Judgement:
The question before us is not one of democratic legitimacy in its ceremonial form, but of whether the structural conditions for voluntary submission remain intact — for consent that cannot be withdrawn is indistinguishable from capitulation under force.

What I have always insisted upon is that freedom is defined not by the presence of approval but by the permanent possibility of its revision. A government that seals off the mechanisms of dissent — through captured courts, controlled information, or the elimination of genuine alternatives — has transformed consent from an ongoing relationship into a historical artefact, invoked endlessly while becoming impossible to rescind. This is coercion wearing the mask of mandate: the governed are held not by agreement but by the impossibility of disagreement.

A regime that extinguishes the practical means of opposition has answered the question itself, regardless of what founding documents it cites.

*Consent without the power of refusal is not a social contract — it is a bill of sale.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Consent that cannot be withdrawn is not consent — it is the vocabulary of liberty pressed into the service of chains, and this question cuts to the very corruption I spent my life exposing.

A government that claims the people's authority while sealing every exit reduces that claim to ceremony. I argued against Burke that hereditary power dressed in the robes of tradition was still despotism; the same holds for elected power dressed in the language of contract. Reason demands that rights carry teeth: the right to consent is hollow unless it includes the right to refuse, to resist, to reconstitute. Where that practical mechanism is denied, what remains is the master's old trick — granting the slave the dignity of a signature on his own bill of sale.

No principle distinguishes such a government from tyranny; it is tyranny with better manners.

*The liberty that cannot be reclaimed was never liberty — only a more elegant form of subjection.*
